newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus leader finalise union charter.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus leader finalise union charter.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko on Thursday finalised the text of a charter for a Union Treaty between their two Slav states, the Kremlin said.
"The two presidents also discussed during their Kremlin meeting some issues concerning the strategic prospective of Russia-Belarus relations," a Kremlin spokesman said.

The spokesman did not elaborate and it was not clear whether Yeltsin and the hardline Belarus president had managed to hammer out the outsanding problems of the planned union or had agreed to put them aside.
Lukashenko made clear before the start of the talks that Belarus would remain a sovereign state, rejecting talk that a closer alliance as some kind of federation could be formed.
"We have a certain limit -- our Soviet experience. Under the Soviet Union we (Belarus) had our own United Nations membership," Lukashenko said before he left Minsk.
Yeltsin said earlier this week that he saw Russia and Belarus merging into a single federative state by the end of the integration process, comments which prompted an angry reaction in Minsk.
Belarus negotiators were seeking a tight union between two independent states, each of which would have equal rights.

Lukashenko's nationalist opponents in Belarus have condemned the planned union as a plot by Moscow to revive the empire and rob Minsk of the independence it won when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
Russian liberals bitterly oppose the union, saying a deal with Lukashenko could hurt Russian democracy and tarnish Russia's image abroad.
But opinion polls show that the majority of the population in both states support the idea of close integration between the two former Soviet republics.

A declarative Union Treaty was signed on April 2 after a last-minute intervention by newly-appointed liberals in the Russian government nervous that the original document gave Lukashenko too much power.
The charter, initialled at the same time, was then opened to public debate but details of what the final version involves have been kept under wraps.

Lukashenko has said he hoped a personal meeting with Yeltsin could clear up remaining differences. But the Russian president clearly indicated before the talks that his capacity for compromise was not endless.
"We have agreed to meet with Lukashenko on May 22, so we do," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
"We will agree everything we need to agree without taking decisions which would contradict the interests of our countries and peoples," Yeltsin said.
